subject: Mathematics
title: Factorise, solve, check
capsTopic: Algebraic expressions; equations and inequalities
notes: Factorising reverses multiplication. Always check for a common factor before trying brackets.
For x² + bx + c, find two numbers with sum b and product c. This shortcut assumes the coefficient of x² is 1.
The zero-product rule applies to a product equal to zero: AB = 0 implies A = 0 or B = 0.

visual.title: Build the brackets

example: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
steps: The numbers −2 and −3 have sum −5 and product 6.
Write (x − 2)(x − 3) = 0. Set each bracket equal to zero.
questions: Factorise 6x² + 9x.
Solve x² + 7x + 12 = 0.
A learner says x² = 9 gives only x = 3. Correct the answer and explain.
answers: 3x(2x + 3). The common factor is 3x.
x = 3 or −3, because squaring either number gives 9.
commonMistake: Do not cancel terms across addition. Only common factors can be cancelled in a fraction.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Mathematics
title: Read a quadratic graph
capsTopic: Functions: quadratic functions
goals: Find intercepts and the turning point
State a range using the turning point
notes: A quadratic graph has equation y = ax² + bx + c, with a ≠ 0. Positive a opens upwards; negative a opens downwards.
The axis of symmetry is x = −b/(2a). Substitute this x-value to find the turning point.
The y-intercept occurs at x = 0. The x-intercepts occur where y = 0; there may be two, one or no real roots.

visual.title: Symmetry around x = 2

example: Sketch y = x² − 4x + 3 and state its range.
steps: Factorise: y = (x − 1)(x − 3), giving roots 1 and 3.
The axis is x = 2; y(2) = −1. Mark (2; −1) and the y-intercept (0; 3).
Draw a smooth upward parabola through these points. The range is y ≥ −1.
questions: Find the roots of y = x² − 6x + 8.
Find its turning point.
State its axis of symmetry and range.
answers: (x − 2)(x − 4) gives x = 2 and x = 4.
x = 3; y = 9 − 18 + 8 = −1. Turning point (3; −1).
Axis x = 3; range y ≥ −1.
commonMistake: The axis of symmetry is an equation x = k, not a single point or a y-value.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Mathematics
title: Differentiate and interpret
capsTopic: Differential calculus: derivatives; cubic functions
goals: Use a sign test to classify turning points
notes: The derivative f′(x) describes the gradient of the tangent. For a power axⁿ, the derivative is anxⁿ⁻¹.
At a stationary point f′(x) = 0. Use f(x), not f′(x), to find the point’s y-coordinate.
A change in f′ from positive to negative indicates a local maximum; negative to positive indicates a local minimum.

visual.title: Gradient sign chart for f(x) = x³ − 3x

example: Find and classify the stationary points of f(x) = x³ − 3x.
steps: f′(x) = 3x² − 3. Set 3(x² − 1) = 0, so x = −1 or 1.
f(−1) = 2 and f(1) = −2. The points are (−1; 2) and (1; −2).
The derivative changes + to − at −1: local maximum. It changes − to + at 1: local minimum.
questions: Differentiate 2x³ − 5x² + 4.
Find the gradient of its tangent at x = 2.
Find the tangent equation there.
answers: 6x² − 10x. The derivative of the constant is zero.
commonMistake: f′(a) is a gradient, not the height of the graph. Find f(a) separately.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Mathematical Literacy
title: A budget that balances
capsTopic: Finance: income, expenditure and budgets
notes: A budget estimates money received and spent over the same period. Actual spending may differ from planned spending.
Fixed expenses are usually agreed amounts; variable expenses depend on use. A surplus is income minus expenses when the result is positive.
Compare like periods and units. Include transport, food and data before treating an apparent surplus as available savings.

visual.title: One learner’s monthly plan

example: Use the plan to calculate the balance and test whether saving R250 is feasible.
steps: Balance = R1 200 − R1 000 = R200.
Saving R250 needs another R50. Reduce an affordable expense or increase income; do not assume essential transport can disappear.
questions: Income is R2 000 and expenses R1 750. Calculate the surplus.
Data spending rises from R150 to R180. Find the increase as a percentage.
A weekly expense is R50. Estimate its cost over a stated four-week month.
answers: R200 for four weeks. A calendar month is not always exactly four weeks.
commonMistake: A surplus is a money amount. A percentage increase uses the original amount as its denominator.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Mathematical Literacy
title: Compare tariffs fairly
capsTopic: Finance: tariffs and financial documents
goals: Calculate a bill with a fixed and variable part
Interpret a break-even point in context
notes: A tariff may have a fixed fee plus a charge per unit. Write down both parts before calculating.
Use the same usage and billing period for each option. A cheaper per-unit rate may still cost more at low usage.
A mathematical break-even value is a comparison tool; actual contracts may also have limits, taxes and once-off fees.

visual.title: Illustrative data tariffs — not network offers

example: Which plan costs less at 8 GB? At what usage do the bills match?
steps: A costs 50 + 10 × 8 = R130. B costs 20 × 8 = R160.
At break-even, 50 + 10u = 20u, so u = 5 GB and both cost R100.
Below 5 GB B is cheaper; above 5 GB A is cheaper, under these simplified tariff rules.
questions: Calculate A at 12 GB.
How much is saved using A instead of B at 12 GB?
Why should a buyer still inspect the full contract?
answers: B costs R240, so the saving is R70.
Possible fair-use limits, coverage, fees, expiry and contract terms may affect the decision.
commonMistake: Do not multiply the fixed fee by the number of units.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Mathematical Literacy
title: Interpret financial growth
capsTopic: Finance: interest and inflation
notes: Simple interest is calculated on the original principal. Compound interest adds interest to the balance before the next period.
For annual compounding use A = P(1 + i)ⁿ, with i as a decimal and n in years. A different compounding period needs a matching rate and number of periods.
Inflation describes rising prices. A higher money balance does not guarantee greater purchasing power; compare growth over the same period.

visual.title: R1 000 at an illustrative 10% per year

example: Calculate the balance on R2 000 at 8% compounded annually for two years.
steps: Interest earned = 2 332.80 − 2 000 = R332.80. This example excludes fees and tax.
questions: Calculate simple interest on R2 000 at 8% for two years.
A basket rises from R500 to R540. Calculate inflation for that basket.
If income stays R5 000 while prices rise, what happens to purchasing power?
answers: It falls: the same income buys fewer goods, assuming the price changes apply to those goods.
commonMistake: 8% must be entered as 0.08 in a growth formula, not as 8.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Physical Sciences
title: Motion in one dimension
capsTopic: Mechanics: instantaneous speed and velocity; acceleration
notes: Distance is total path length, a scalar. Displacement is final position minus initial position, a vector with a chosen positive direction.
Average velocity equals displacement divided by elapsed time. Average speed uses total distance instead.
On a position–time graph, gradient represents velocity. A horizontal line means the position is constant, not necessarily zero.

visual.title: A walker returns towards the start; east is positive

example: The walker moves 4 m east in 2 s, then 4 m west in 2 s. Find average speed and velocity.
steps: Distance = 4 + 4 = 8 m; displacement = 0 − 0 = 0 m.
Elapsed time = 4 s, so average speed = 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m·s⁻¹.
Average velocity = 0 ÷ 4 = 0 m·s⁻¹. Motion occurred even though net displacement is zero.
questions: A cyclist travels 30 m east in 5 s. Find average velocity.
Velocity changes from 2 to 8 m·s⁻¹ east in 3 s. Find acceleration.
Explain the gradient of a downward-sloping position–time line.
answers: 6 m·s⁻¹ east.
Velocity is negative relative to the chosen positive direction; it does not automatically mean slowing down.
commonMistake: Use m·s⁻² for acceleration. A negative velocity describes direction, not automatically a decrease in speed.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending
furtherReading: Siyavula Grade 10 Physical Sciences Learner Book, chapter 21: speed and velocity (indexed PDF page 412; printed page 396). Available in the signed-in resource search. Original publisher attribution retained.

subject: Physical Sciences
title: Forces and Newton’s second law
capsTopic: Mechanics: Newton’s laws and application
goals: Apply Fnet = ma with a sign convention
notes: A free-body diagram isolates one object and shows forces acting on it, not forces it exerts on other objects.
Choose a positive direction. Resolve and add forces along that axis before applying Fnet = ma.
On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, normal force balances weight if there are no other vertical forces. Friction acts against relative motion or its tendency.

visual.title: Free-body inventory: 5 kg crate pulled horizontally

example: Find the horizontal acceleration of the crate. Use g = 9.8 m·s⁻².
steps: Take right as positive. Vertical resultant = 49 − 49 = 0 N.
Horizontal resultant = 20 − 5 = 15 N right.
a = Fnet/m = 15/5 = 3 m·s⁻² right.
questions: A 4 kg trolley has a net force of 12 N left. Find acceleration.
What resultant force keeps an object at constant velocity?
Are weight and normal force a Newton’s third-law pair? Explain.
answers: 3 m·s⁻² left.
Zero resultant force; individual forces may still act.
No. They act on the same object. A third-law pair acts on two different objects.
commonMistake: Never use the applied force alone in Fnet = ma when friction or other forces also act.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Physical Sciences
title: Momentum and collisions
capsTopic: Mechanics: momentum and impulse
goals: Apply conservation to a closed system
Relate impulse to force and time
notes: Momentum p = mv is a vector. Select a positive direction and give opposite velocities opposite signs.
The total momentum of an isolated system is conserved. In a collision, use the condition of negligible net external impulse.
Impulse equals change in momentum: FnetΔt = Δp. Momentum conservation does not imply kinetic energy conservation in an inelastic collision.

visual.title: Two trolleys stick together; right is positive

example: A 2 kg trolley moving right at 3 m·s⁻¹ sticks to a stationary 1 kg trolley. Find their final velocity.
steps: Before: total momentum = 2(3) + 1(0) = 6 kg·m·s⁻¹.
After: the combined mass is 3 kg, so 6 = 3v and v = 2 m·s⁻¹ right.
Initial kinetic energy is 9 J; final kinetic energy is 6 J. The 3 J difference becomes other energy forms.
questions: Find the momentum of a 0.5 kg ball moving left at 4 m·s⁻¹, taking right as positive.
It rebounds right at 6 m·s⁻¹. Find Δp.
If contact lasts 0.1 s, find the average net force.
answers: −2 kg·m·s⁻¹.
Final momentum = +3; change = 3 − (−2) = +5 kg·m·s⁻¹.
Fnet = 5/0.1 = 50 N right.
commonMistake: Change means final minus initial. Reversing direction requires a negative initial or final velocity.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Life Sciences
title: Cells: structure explains function
capsTopic: Life at the molecular, cellular and tissue level: cells
goals: Relate an organelle to its function
Compare typical plant and animal cells
notes: Cells are the basic structural and functional units of living organisms. A cell membrane controls movement of substances into and out of the cell.
The nucleus contains genetic material. Mitochondria are sites of aerobic cellular respiration; they transfer energy into usable chemical forms.
Typical plant cells have a cellulose cell wall and a large central vacuole. Photosynthetic plant cells contain chloroplasts; not every plant cell has chloroplasts.

visual.title: Compare structures, not just outlines

example: A micrograph shows a rigid outer layer and many chloroplasts. Explain the most likely cell type.
steps: The rigid outer layer is consistent with a cell wall.
Chloroplasts support photosynthesis, indicating a photosynthetic plant cell.
Use the observed structures as evidence; a rectangular shape alone is not enough to identify a cell reliably.
questions: Name the structure that controls movement across a cell boundary.
Explain why muscle cells need many mitochondria.
A drawing is 40 mm long and the actual cell is 0.1 mm. Calculate magnification.
answers: The cell membrane.
Muscle contraction needs energy; mitochondria support aerobic respiration and ATP production.
Magnification = drawing size / actual size = 40/0.1 = 400 times.
commonMistake: Do not say mitochondria create energy. They transfer energy during cellular respiration.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending
furtherReading: Siyavula Grade 10 Life Sciences Learner Book, chapter 3: cell structures (indexed PDF pages 79–81). Available in the signed-in resource search. Original publisher attribution retained.

subject: Life Sciences
title: Photosynthesis: test an explanation
capsTopic: Life processes in plants and animals: photosynthesis
notes: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen. Chlorophyll absorbs light in chloroplasts.
A limiting factor restricts the rate even when other requirements are available. Increasing light may eventually stop increasing the rate if another factor becomes limiting.
A fair investigation changes one independent variable, measures a dependent variable and controls other relevant conditions. Repeat measurements to improve reliability.

visual.title: Illustrative pondweed results

example: Interpret the results and identify one weakness of counting bubbles.
steps: As lamp distance increases, bubble count falls, suggesting reduced photosynthesis as light decreases.
Distance is changed; bubble count is measured. Keep plant size, water temperature and carbon dioxide availability controlled.
Bubble sizes vary, so counts are an imperfect estimate of oxygen volume. Measuring gas volume over time gives a stronger comparison.
questions: Name two raw materials of photosynthesis.
Why might a lamp heat confound the investigation?
Why does a rate plateau not mean that photosynthesis has stopped?
answers: Carbon dioxide and water.
Temperature also affects enzyme-controlled reactions, so the result may reflect two changing variables.
The rate can remain positive but constant because another factor limits further increase.
commonMistake: Glucose is a product; sunlight supplies energy and is not a raw material with mass in the equation.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Life Sciences
title: Monohybrid inheritance
capsTopic: Genetics and inheritance: monohybrid crosses
notes: Alleles are alternative forms of a gene. In a simple complete-dominance model, one dominant allele is enough for the dominant phenotype.
Genotype describes the allele combination; phenotype is the observable characteristic. A heterozygote has two different alleles.
Each fertilisation is a new probability event. Expected ratios describe many offspring, not a guaranteed sequence within one family.

visual.title: Tt × Tt: each parent forms T and t gametes

example: In a hypothetical plant, T is dominant for tall growth and t is recessive for short growth. Cross two heterozygotes.
steps: Parents: Tt × Tt. Each produces T and t gametes.
The combinations are TT, Tt, Tt and tt: genotype ratio 1 : 2 : 1.
Tall offspring probability = 3/4; short = 1/4. Phenotype ratio is 3 tall : 1 short under the stated model.
questions: Cross Tt with tt and list the offspring genotypes.
State the probability of short offspring in that cross.
Explain why two tall parents can produce a short offspring.
answers: Tt, tt, Tt, tt: 1 Tt : 1 tt.
Both may be heterozygous and each may contribute a recessive t allele, producing tt.
commonMistake: Dominant does not mean more common, stronger or better. State the inheritance model before interpreting a ratio.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Accounting
title: Keep the accounting equation in balance
capsTopic: Financial accounting: accounting equation and double entry
notes: The accounting equation is Assets = Owner’s equity + Liabilities. Every transaction must preserve this relationship.
Assets are controlled resources; liabilities are obligations. Capital contributed increases owner’s equity; drawings decrease it.
Buying an asset for cash changes the mix of assets without necessarily changing total assets. A loan increases both cash and liabilities.

visual.title: A new business: transaction effects

example: Calculate the balances after all three transactions in the table.
steps: Total assets = R12 000. Equity = R10 000 and liabilities = R2 000.
Check: 12 000 = 10 000 + 2 000. Equipment was not an expense in this purchase.
questions: The owner withdraws R500 cash for personal use. State the equation effects.
The business pays R200 cash for electricity. State the effects.
Why is a bank loan not income?
answers: Assets decrease R500; equity decreases R500 through drawings; liabilities unchanged.
Assets and equity each decrease R200; electricity is an expense.
It must be repaid and creates a liability, rather than earned revenue.
commonMistake: Cash received is not always income: it can be capital, a loan or payment of an existing debtor.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Accounting
title: Partnership profit appropriation
capsTopic: Financial accounting: partnerships
notes: In a school partnership appropriation calculation, partners’ salaries and interest on capital allocate profit according to the agreement.
Deduct the agreed appropriations from net profit to find residual profit. Divide the residual using the agreed profit-sharing ratio.
A partner’s drawings are not a business operating expense. Keep capital, current accounts and cash movements distinct.

visual.title: Illustrative agreement and annual allocation

example: Net profit is R100 000. Use the table to calculate each partner’s total appropriation.
steps: Total salary and interest = 30 000 + 20 000 + 5 000 + 3 000 = R58 000.
A total = R60 200; B total = R39 800. Their totals reconcile to R100 000.
questions: Calculate 10% interest on capital of R80 000 for a full year.
Split residual profit R25 000 in the ratio 2 : 3.
Why should partner drawings not reduce net profit?
answers: R10 000 and R15 000 respectively.
Drawings are withdrawals by owners, not costs incurred to earn business revenue.
commonMistake: Do not apply the residual sharing ratio to the whole net profit before the agreed salaries and interest.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Accounting
title: Use ratios to explain performance
capsTopic: Financial accounting: companies; analysis and interpretation
goals: Calculate gross profit and liquidity ratios
notes: Gross profit is sales less cost of sales. Gross profit margin = gross profit / sales × 100; mark-up on cost uses cost of sales as denominator.
Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities. Acid-test ratio excludes inventory from current assets in the simplified school calculation.
Ratios need comparison with prior periods, targets or context. A high current ratio can include slow-moving stock and does not automatically mean cash is available.

visual.title: Illustrative company information

example: Calculate gross profit margin, current ratio and acid-test ratio.
steps: Current ratio = 120 000 : 60 000 = 2 : 1.
Acid-test = (120 000 − 40 000) : 60 000 = 1.33 : 1, rounded to two decimals.
questions: Calculate the mark-up on cost for the same company.
If inventory rises while cash falls by the same amount, what happens to current ratio?
Give one reason acid-test ratio may still overstate immediate cash availability.
answers: It is unchanged if total current assets and liabilities stay the same, although asset quality changes.
Debtors may pay late or not pay; receivables are not immediately available cash.
commonMistake: Always label the ratio and denominator. Gross profit margin and mark-up are different measures.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Business Studies
title: Know the business environments
capsTopic: Business environments: micro, market and macro
notes: The micro environment is inside the business: its vision, resources and functions. Management usually has substantial control over it.
The market environment includes customers, suppliers and competitors. A business can influence relationships but cannot fully control these parties.
The macro environment includes wider economic, social, technological and other external forces. Businesses usually adapt to these rather than control them.

visual.title: Three lenses for a school stationery shop

example: A stationery shop loses sales because staff arrive late and a competitor offers delivery. Classify and respond.
steps: Late staff: micro environment. The owner can set attendance expectations and improve scheduling.
Competitor delivery: market environment. The owner can investigate customer needs and offer a feasible delivery option.
Explain why the response fits the cause instead of giving the same generic recommendation for both.
questions: Classify a new internal staff training programme.
Classify a new competing shop.
Why can a small shop not simply eliminate economy-wide inflation?
answers: Micro: internal skills and staffing.
Market: a competitor operates in the external market.
Inflation is a wider economic influence beyond the individual firm’s control; the firm must adapt.
commonMistake: An event outside the premises is not automatically macro. Customers and suppliers belong to the market environment.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Business Studies
title: Turn a challenge into an action plan
capsTopic: Business ventures: creative thinking and problem solving
goals: Separate a symptom from a cause
notes: Problem solving begins by defining a specific problem and gathering evidence. A fall in sales is a symptom until its causes are investigated.
Generate alternatives before selecting one. Compare likely benefits, costs, time and risks instead of choosing the first idea.
Implementation needs an owner, deadline and measurable result. Review evidence afterwards and adjust if the solution does not work.

visual.title: A structured problem-solving cycle
rows: late orders after new stock rule

example: A small business has 20 late orders, 15 caused by stock-outs. Recommend a justified first intervention.
steps: The evidence points to stock availability as the main measured cause, not necessarily unmotivated staff.
Compare a reorder-level system with holding much more stock. The first may reduce cash tied up but needs accurate records.
Assign the stock controller a two-week trial and compare the late-order count, while checking demand changes.
questions: Why should customer complaints be analysed before selecting a solution?
Give one disadvantage of carrying excess stock.
Name a measurable indicator for a trial delivery improvement.
answers: To identify patterns and causes instead of guessing from isolated symptoms.
It ties up cash and risks damage, obsolescence or storage costs.
Percentage of orders delivered on time over a stated period, compared with a baseline.
commonMistake: A recommendation without a responsible person, time frame or success measure is incomplete as an action plan.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Business Studies
title: Match a strategy to the challenge
capsTopic: Business environments: business strategies; SWOT analysis
goals: Distinguish internal and external SWOT factors
notes: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external. A SWOT list should use specific evidence.
Strategy responds to the business situation. Options may include development, integration, diversification or defensive measures, depending on the case.
An exam response needs a clear recommendation and application to the scenario. Consider affordability, risk and likely outcomes rather than assuming expansion always works.

visual.title: SWOT for an illustrative tutoring publisher

example: The publisher has strong authors but slow delivery and little cash. Recommend a cautious response to demand for digital notes.
steps: Use the author strength to pilot a small digital product rather than attempting every subject immediately.
A pilot can reduce delivery delays and limit upfront costs, but requires editing and reliable access.
Evaluate download completion, learner feedback and contribution to costs before expanding.
questions: Classify a cash shortage in SWOT.
Classify a new competitor offering free content.
Give two criteria for evaluating the digital pilot.
answers: Weakness: an internal resource limitation.
Threat: an external competitive influence.
For example, completed downloads and learner usefulness ratings; also compare costs with revenue or funding.
commonMistake: Naming a strategy earns little without explaining why it addresses the specific challenge in the case.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Economics
title: Follow the circular flow
capsTopic: Macroeconomics: circular flow and economic participants
notes: In a simple closed two-sector model, households supply factors of production and firms produce goods and services.
Factor payments such as wages flow from firms to households. Consumption spending flows from households to firms.
Real flows and money flows move in opposite directions. This simplified model excludes government, financial and foreign sectors; real economies include them.

visual.title: Two markets connect households and firms

example: A learner’s household earns R4 000 from a bakery and spends R600 on bread. Identify the flows.
steps: Labour supplied to the bakery is a real factor flow from household to firm.
The R4 000 wage is a money flow from firm to household.
Bread moves from firm to household, while the R600 spending moves in the opposite direction.
questions: Name two factors of production besides labour.
Is a wage a real flow or a money flow?
Explain why lower household spending may affect firms.
answers: Land, capital or entrepreneurship; any two.
A money flow: payment for labour.
It can reduce firms’ sales revenue, which may affect production and demand for factors.
commonMistake: In economics, capital as a production factor means produced tools and equipment, rather than simply any cash balance.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Economics
title: Price elasticity and related markets
capsTopic: Microeconomics: price elasticity; relationships between markets
goals: Connect a cost change to a related market
notes: Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a price change, other things equal. Use the magnitude of percentage change in quantity divided by percentage change in price.

Using original-value percentages, an elasticity greater than 1 is elastic; less than 1 is inelastic; equal to 1 is unit elastic. State the method used because different percentage conventions can produce different results.
Markets are linked. A rise in a key input price can increase production costs and reduce product supply, other things equal. A product’s own price change is a movement along its demand curve.

visual.title: Illustrative notebook market: original-value percentage method

example: Use the table to calculate price elasticity of demand and explain the revenue change.
steps: Elasticity magnitude = 20/10 = 2. Demand is elastic over this change using the stated method.
Revenue falls from 10 × 100 = R1 000 to 11 × 80 = R880 because the proportional quantity fall exceeds the price increase.
questions: Price rises 5% and quantity demanded falls 2%. Calculate elasticity magnitude.
Classify the demand response in question 1.
Explain how a rise in paper prices can affect notebook supply.
answers: Inelastic, because the elasticity magnitude is less than 1.
Paper is an input. Higher input costs can reduce notebook supply, shifting its supply curve left, other things equal.
commonMistake: Calculate percentage changes before dividing. Dividing raw quantities by rand amounts does not give price elasticity.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Economics
title: Interpret the multiplier
capsTopic: Macroeconomics: circular flow; the multiplier
notes: The marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is the share of additional income spent on consumption. In the simple model MPS = 1 − MPC.
The simple closed-economy multiplier is k = 1/(1 − MPC). An initial autonomous expenditure change has a modelled total income effect ΔY = kΔA.
This is a simplified model without taxes or imports and with capacity to expand output. It does not promise that any real policy achieves the calculated result.

visual.title: An initial R100 spending injection with MPC = 0.8

example: MPC is 0.8 and autonomous investment increases by R20 million. Calculate the simple income effect.
steps: k = 1/0.2 = 5. Therefore ΔY = 5 × R20 million = R100 million.
The result includes the original injection and later spending rounds; it is conditional on the model assumptions.
questions: Calculate k when MPC = 0.75.
Calculate the effect of a R10 million injection using that k.
How would additional import leakages tend to affect the multiplier?
answers: ΔY = 4 × 10 = R40 million.
They tend to reduce the domestic income multiplier because some spending goes abroad.
commonMistake: The multiplier is not MPC itself, and the total effect must not be added to the initial injection a second time.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Tourism
title: Understand the tourism system
capsTopic: Tourism sectors; domestic tourism
notes: A domestic tourist travels within their country of residence outside their usual environment. International tourism crosses a national border.
Tourism relies on connected sectors such as transport, accommodation, attractions, food services and travel distribution.
Good planning considers accessibility, safety, realistic travel time and visitors’ needs. Do not assume all tourists have the same budget or physical access requirements.

visual.title: A domestic weekend trip

example: A family living in Gauteng visits a museum in the Western Cape and stays two nights. Classify the trip and identify three sectors.
steps: The trip is domestic because residence and destination are within South Africa.
Transport gets the family there; accommodation provides the overnight stay; the museum is an attraction.
Check opening times and travel distance before promising an itinerary; actual prices and schedules must be verified.
questions: A resident of Botswana visits South Africa. Is this domestic tourism for South Africa?
Name a tourism service supplied by a travel agent.
Give one way a local tourism business can support its community.
answers: No; it is inbound international tourism for South Africa.
For example, arranging transport and accommodation bookings.
Employ locally, source suitable goods locally or partner fairly with community guides.
commonMistake: Nationality and country of residence are different. Tourism classifications use the stated travel context.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Tourism
title: Build a responsible itinerary
capsTopic: Tour planning; responsible and sustainable tourism
notes: An itinerary sequences travel, activities and rest with realistic buffers. Check actual access, opening times and booking requirements.
A budget separates per-person costs from shared costs. State the number of travellers, nights and any exclusions.
Responsible tourism aims to reduce harm and support local benefits while providing a good visitor experience. Claims should be tied to specific actions, not vague green labels.

visual.title: Illustrative one-night trip for two people

example: Calculate the total and per-person cost, then suggest one responsible choice.
steps: Shared equally, cost per person = 1 940/2 = R970; this excludes any unstated fees.
Use an appropriately qualified local guide and follow site rules; explain how the choice supports livelihoods or protects the destination.
questions: Add a 10% contingency to the total.
Why must a four-hour journey not be scheduled as a one-hour transfer?
Name one measurable action that reduces waste.
answers: R194 contingency; revised total R2 134.
It makes later activities infeasible and may encourage unsafe rushing.
For example, provide refillable water bottles and measure fewer single-use bottles used.
commonMistake: Do not charge a shared room twice per person unless the quotation explicitly gives a per-person rate.
reviewStatus: Editorial draft — subject teacher review pending

subject: Tourism
title: Time zones without guesswork
capsTopic: Map work and tour planning: time zones and travel calculations
notes: UTC offsets state how far local time is ahead of or behind UTC. Convert departure time to UTC first, then add elapsed flight time.
Convert the arrival UTC time to the destination’s stated offset. Adjust the date whenever the calculation crosses midnight.
Use the offsets supplied in an exam. For real bookings verify the actual date-specific local time, because some destinations use seasonal clock changes.

visual.title: Worked route with stated offsets

example: A flight leaves Johannesburg at 22:00 on Monday, flies 10 hours and arrives at a destination on UTC+1. Find arrival time and day.

01:00 the next day.

subject: History
title: Explain the French Revolution
capsTopic: The French Revolution: causes and historical skills
goals: Distinguish a long-term cause from a trigger
Evaluate the limits of a source
notes: Before 1789, French society was divided into estates with unequal privileges. Social inequality and debates about political authority contributed to criticism of the old order.
State debt and a fiscal crisis increased pressure for reform. Harvest failures and high bread prices intensified popular hardship.
A revolution has interacting causes. A single event can trigger action without explaining the longer processes that made it possible.

visual.title: Selected sequence — not a complete chronology

example: Explain how financial crisis and inequality could combine to weaken the monarchy.
steps: Debt and difficulties raising revenue made the government seek fiscal and political solutions.
Unequal privileges made reform contentious and encouraged demands for fairer representation and taxation.
Connect these pressures: a financial problem opened a political confrontation in an already unequal society.
questions: Name one long-term social cause.
Why is the storming of the Bastille insufficient as the only explanation for revolution?
What should you check before using a political cartoon as evidence?
answers: The unequal privileges and burdens of the estate system.
It describes an event but does not explain the prior social, fiscal and political conditions.
Creator, date, intended audience, purpose, symbols and what the cartoon can and cannot show.
commonMistake: A source can be useful even when partisan; identify what its perspective reveals and corroborate factual claims.

subject: History
title: Explain the Russian revolutions
capsTopic: Communism in Russia, 1900–1940: revolutions of 1917
goals: Distinguish an event from an interpretation
notes: Russia’s involvement in the First World War intensified military, economic and political pressures. Food shortages and discontent weakened confidence in tsarist rule.
The February Revolution led to the abdication of Nicholas II. The Provisional Government faced continuing war and competing political authority.
In the October Revolution the Bolsheviks took power. Explaining this outcome requires attention to government weaknesses, political organisation and popular demands.

visual.title: Conventional names use the old Russian calendar
rows: how did they gain support and act?

example: Explain why ending tsarist rule did not immediately resolve Russia’s crisis.
steps: The February Revolution changed political leadership but inherited war and shortages.
Continuing involvement in the war sustained hardship and discontent.
Rival centres of authority and competing programmes made effective government difficult; political change alone did not remove the underlying pressures.
questions: Identify the ruler who abdicated in 1917.
Why should a historian compare a Bolshevik slogan with other evidence?
Give one reason not to merge February and October into a single event.
answers: Nicholas II.
A slogan reveals political aims and persuasion, but not by itself actual support or implementation.
They removed different authorities and occurred in different political circumstances.
commonMistake: The conventional February and October names refer to the Julian calendar then used in Russia; dates differ in the Gregorian calendar.

title: Civil resistance and historical argument
capsTopic: Civil resistance in South Africa, 1970s–1980s

subject: Geography
title: Atmosphere: explain heating
capsTopic: The atmosphere: heating of the atmosphere
notes: The Sun supplies mainly shortwave radiation. Some is reflected; some is absorbed by the atmosphere and surface.
The warmed Earth emits longwave infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit some outgoing infrared, helping warm the lower atmosphere and surface.
Albedo is reflectivity. A brighter surface generally reflects more incoming radiation, while a darker surface generally absorbs more under comparable conditions.

visual.title: Simplified energy pathway

example: Why might dark tar warm more than a pale painted surface in sunshine?
steps: Compare surfaces under the same sunlight and other similar conditions.
Dark tar generally has a lower albedo and absorbs a larger share of incoming radiation.
More absorbed energy can raise its temperature; wind, moisture and material properties also affect actual temperatures.
questions: Which has higher albedo: fresh snow or dark tar?
Name the radiation mainly emitted by the Earth.
Why is the greenhouse effect different from ozone depletion?
answers: Fresh snow.
Longwave infrared radiation.
The greenhouse effect concerns infrared absorption and re-emission; ozone depletion concerns reduced protection from harmful ultraviolet radiation.
commonMistake: Do not explain global warming as the ozone hole letting in extra heat; these are different atmospheric processes.

subject: Geography
title: Use development indicators critically
capsTopic: Development geography: indicators and development
notes: Development involves changes in living conditions and opportunities, not only economic output.
GDP per capita divides output by population. It is an average and does not describe how income is distributed.
Use several indicators, such as life expectancy, education and access to services. Compare the same year, units and methods before drawing conclusions.

visual.title: Invented data for comparison practice

example: Can you conclude that A is more developed simply because its GDP per capita is higher?
steps: A has the higher measured average output per person.
B has higher life expectancy and water access in this invented dataset.
A single indicator cannot justify the full conclusion. Assess distribution, social outcomes and data quality before comparing development.
questions: Output is R600 million and population 10 000. Find output per person.
Why can two places with equal GDP per capita have different living standards?
Name one limitation of comparing indicators from different years.
answers: R60 000 per person.
Distribution, public services, costs and other conditions may differ.
Economic or demographic changes can make the figures non-comparable over time.
commonMistake: GDP per capita is not each person’s salary and does not prove that benefits are equally shared.

subject: Geography
title: Read a river’s long profile
capsTopic: Geomorphology: fluvial processes; river profiles
notes: A river’s long profile shows elevation along its course. It commonly becomes gentler downstream, although local geology and disturbances create exceptions.
Erosion removes material, transport moves it and deposition occurs when the river can no longer carry part of its load.
In a meander, faster flow commonly erodes the outer bank while slower flow deposits material on the inner bank. Distinguish this cross-sectional pattern from the river’s long profile.

visual.title: Simplified downstream pattern

example: Explain why the outside and inside banks of a meander may change differently.
steps: Flow is commonly faster and deeper near the outer bank, promoting erosion and a river cliff.
Slower flow near the inner bank encourages deposition and a slip-off slope.
Over time this can move the meander laterally. Real outcomes also depend on discharge, sediment and bank material.
questions: Define deposition.
A river falls 120 m over 6 km. Calculate average gradient as a ratio in the same units.
Why does gentler gradient not always mean lower discharge?
answers: The laying down of sediment when transport capacity is insufficient to carry that load.
Discharge depends on cross-sectional area and velocity; tributaries may increase volume downstream.
commonMistake: Convert kilometres to metres before forming the gradient ratio. A profile is not a plan view of a winding river.

subject: English HL
title: Read closely and quote with purpose
capsTopic: Reading and viewing: comprehension; language in context
goals: Explain a word choice in context
notes: Literal questions ask for information stated directly. Inference combines a textual clue with a reasonable explanation; it is not unsupported guessing.
A quotation supports a point only when you explain how its wording matters. Keep quotations short and relevant.
Tone is the speaker’s attitude. Use the language of the passage to justify your description rather than choosing a tone word from memory.

visual.title: From clue to explanation

example: Original text: “Lindi checked the empty road again. When the bus appeared, she finally exhaled and stepped into its warm light.” Explain Lindi’s likely feelings.
steps: The word “again” suggests repeated checking, supporting an inference of anxious waiting.
“Finally exhaled” suggests relief when the bus arrives.
“Warm light” gives the ending a comforting mood. The text does not establish why she was waiting or where she is going.
questions: What appears on the road?
Explain the effect of “again”.
Does the text prove that the bus was late? Justify.
answers: A bus.
It suggests repeated action and can emphasise anticipation or worry.
No. It shows waiting but gives no timetable or expected arrival time.
commonMistake: Do not invent a backstory. An inference must be supported by the words actually provided.

subject: English HL
title: Analyse persuasion, not just opinion
capsTopic: Reading and viewing: critical language awareness
notes: A persuasive text tries to influence an audience. Identify the intended audience, purpose and specific choices used to persuade.
An assertion states a claim. Evidence provides a basis for judging it; check whether it is relevant and credible.
Loaded language and rhetorical questions can shape emotion. Explain the likely effect in this particular text rather than merely naming a technique.

visual.title: Original poster: “Don’t let our library fade. Join Saturday’s book drive. A single book can open a hundred doors.”

example: Explain how the poster encourages community participation.
steps: “Our” includes readers in a shared community and frames the library as a collective responsibility.
The contrast between “fade” and “open” moves from possible loss to opportunity.
The clear instruction identifies an action, but readers still need practical details such as place, time and acceptable donations.
questions: Identify the poster’s main request.
Is “a hundred doors” reliable numerical evidence? Explain.
Suggest one practical improvement to the poster.
answers: Join Saturday’s book drive.
No. It is figurative language expressing opportunity, not a measured outcome.
Add a verified venue, time and contact or donation requirements.
commonMistake: Identifying a device without explaining its effect does not complete a language-analysis response.

subject: English HL
title: Build a defensible literary paragraph
capsTopic: Reading and viewing: literary response; writing and presenting
notes: A literary response develops a reading of a text. Start with a precise claim that can be defended using its language or structure.
Evidence must be followed by analysis: explain what a word, contrast, image or structural choice contributes to meaning.
For prescribed literature, use the school’s current text and edition. This original short poem is skills practice and is not presented as a prescribed poem.

visual.title: Original poem: “I fold the map. / The road remains. / Beyond the gate, / the morning waits.”

example: Write a paragraph explaining how the poem presents beginning a journey.
steps: Claim: the poem presents beginning as a choice to act despite uncertainty.
Evidence: folding the map ends preparation, but “the road remains”, showing that the journey is still ahead.
Analysis: the personified morning “waits” makes possibility feel available; the open ending does not guarantee success.
questions: Identify one example of personification.
Explain the contrast between the first two lines.
Why is “the speaker will definitely succeed” too strong?
answers: “The morning waits.”
The map can be folded and preparation ended, but the actual road and journey still exist.
The poem offers possibility but gives no outcome; that claim exceeds its evidence.
commonMistake: Distinguish speaker from poet, and interpret from evidence rather than treating every image as having one fixed meaning.

answers: “Ukusa kungilindile.”
Isikhulumi yizwi elikhuluma enkondlweni; asihlali siyimbongi uqobo.
Cha. Inkondlo iveza amathuba kodwa ayisiniki isiphetho sohambo.

subject: Life Orientation
title: Set a goal you can act on
capsTopic: Development of the self in society: self-awareness and goal setting
goals: Turn an aspiration into an action
notes: A useful goal names a specific action and a realistic time frame. Link it to something you value rather than comparing yourself constantly with others.
Planning includes barriers such as transport, data, responsibilities and access to a quiet space. Choose supports that fit your situation.
Review what happened, identify an obstacle and adjust the plan. Reflection is evidence for a better next step, not proof of your worth as a person.

visual.title: From aspiration to a weekly action
rows: practise three factorising questions on Tue/Thu

example: A learner wants to “do better” but has limited data. Turn this into a workable one-week plan.
steps: Choose a small topic and download or print questions when Wi-Fi is available.
Set two short practice sessions and a Friday answer check, allowing for other responsibilities.
Ask a tutor or teacher about one specific error; adjust next week’s plan using the result.
questions: Rewrite “I will study everything tomorrow” as a realistic action.
Name one support besides paid tutoring.
What should you do if the first plan was unrealistic?
answers: For example: complete three algebra questions after school on Tuesday and check them on Wednesday.
A teacher, peer study group, school library or trusted adult.
Identify the barrier, reduce or reschedule the action and review again.
commonMistake: A plan is not effective merely because it is ambitious. It needs feasible actions, support and a way to review progress.

subject: Life Orientation
title: Make an informed study-path decision
capsTopic: Careers and career choices: requirements and opportunities
goals: Connect interests with possible study paths
notes: A career decision combines interests, strengths, values, subject choices and practical constraints. One test or mark should not define your whole future.
Entry requirements differ by institution, programme and year. Check official sources for subject requirements, selection rules and deadlines.
Meeting minimum requirements does not guarantee admission. Keep alternative pathways and investigate funding, accommodation and support.

visual.title: A comparison sheet to complete using official sources

example: A learner enjoys science but has not checked programme requirements. What should they do before applying?
steps: List two suitable programmes and identify each institution’s official admissions page.
Record required subjects, marks, selection steps and the current application deadline with the date checked.
Compare affordability and support, prepare documents and keep a realistic alternative pathway.
questions: Why are social-media posts insufficient as the only admissions source?
Distinguish eligibility from acceptance.
Name two costs besides tuition to investigate.
answers: Posts may be outdated, incomplete or unofficial; verify using the institution.
Eligibility meets stated entry conditions; acceptance is the institution’s actual offer after selection.
For example accommodation, transport, data, books or meals.
commonMistake: Do not publish or reuse an old deadline as current. Always verify the programme and year directly.

subject: Life Orientation
title: Prepare for assessments sustainably
capsTopic: Study skills: examination preparation and stress management
notes: Retrieval practice means trying to recall or apply knowledge before checking notes. Checking errors afterwards helps choose the next revision task.
A balanced revision plan rotates subjects, includes breaks and protects sleep. Long hours alone do not prove that learning has occurred.
Stress can affect concentration. Use practical supports and talk to a trusted adult or qualified professional when distress is persistent or interferes with daily life.

visual.title: A repeatable revision cycle
rows: answer a short set without notes

example: A learner rereads notes for hours but struggles with questions. Suggest a stronger revision session.
steps: Choose a short topic and attempt a few questions before looking at the notes.
Mark the attempt, classify errors as concept, calculation or interpretation, and explain one correction.
Return to a similar question after a gap and ask for help if the concept remains unclear.
questions: Why is copying a memo not enough evidence of learning?
Name one adjustment that can reduce revision overload.
How can a learner use a teacher’s feedback?
answers: It does not show that the learner can recall or apply the reasoning independently.
Reduce session length, prioritise a specific topic, schedule breaks or seek help planning.
Identify a specific recurring error, practise the relevant skill and check the improvement.
commonMistake: Peer advice and study plans do not replace professional support for persistent distress or significant health concerns.
